notes: Laminated flooring patent appeal; claim construction, infringement and G 2/98 priority analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Patent claim construction of 'free of play' in snap-fit flooring panels

statutes_considered.title: Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property

key_facts: Unilin's EP(UK) 1 024 234 concerned snap-fit laminated floor panels with mechanical locking means formed from MDF/HDF.
Judge Fysh QC held claim 20 infringed and was valid; defendants challenged construction of 'free of play', infringement and priority.
Defendants no longer contested non-obviousness on appeal.
The priority document disclosed 'free of play' together with lip-length and thickness features later in claims 19 and 21.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a patent infringement trial concerning proposed amended claim 1 incorporating claim 20's 'free of play' limitation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; 'free of play' construed as sufficiently free of play for practical purposes; amended claim entitled to priority; infringement upheld.
enrichment.ratio: 'Free of play' in the flooring patent means sufficiently free of play to prevent visible gaps in practice, not absolute zero play; under G 2/98/Biogen the priority document as a whole enabled the free-of-play feature independently of lip-length and thickness limitations; consistory clauses in priority documents are not determinative of priority.
legal_issues: Construction of 'free of play' in claim 20
Whether Berry Floor products infringed on any construction
Whether claim 20 was entitled to the first priority date
Relationship between priority document consistory clause and claim scope

notes: CCRC second appeal on discredited West Midlands drug squad officers; Pendleton test applied throughout.

enrichment.short_title: Safety of drug convictions despite later discrediting of police witnesses
key_facts: Deans was convicted in 1989 of drug supply and related offences based largely on West Midlands Central Drug Squad evidence.
A first appeal was dismissed in 1995; the CCRC later referred the case because officers including DC Robotham and DC Breakwell had been discredited.
The prosecution case depended on disputed identification, planted drugs allegations and notebook evidence.
Subsequent misconduct by officers occurred years after the 1988 events, notably Robotham's 1997 theft of cannabis from a suspect.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal following CCRC reference on fresh evidence of subsequent discreditable conduct by police witnesses at the original trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions held safe despite subsequent police misconduct.
enrichment.ratio: Subsequent discreditable conduct by police witnesses can in principle render a conviction unsafe, but a long gap between trial and later misconduct, combined with corroborated evidence from other officers and the limited role of some discredited witnesses, may leave convictions safe; the Pendleton test asks whether fresh evidence might reasonably have affected the jury's decision.
legal_issues: Whether subsequent police misconduct rendered 1989 convictions unsafe
Application of the Pendleton test to fresh evidence
Whether discreditable conduct of one officer infects evidence of others
Temporal gap between trial and subsequent misconduct

notes: Possession claim against charging order; constructive trust and TOLATA sale powers clearly analysed.

enrichment.short_title: Constructive trust life interest resisting possession after undervalue flat transfer

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Solicitors sought possession of a St John's Wood flat to enforce charging orders exceeding £200,000 against barrister Jonathan Steinberg.
Mrs Steinberg, aged 83 and resident since 1959, claimed a rent-free life interest after the flat was sold by the family company to her son at undervalue in 1981.
The 1981 sale used a fictional sitting tenant valuation to reduce price and stamp duty; Jonathan wrote assuring his mother she could remain for life.
Mrs Steinberg abstained from blocking the company sale and signed mortgage postponement documents in reliance on those assurances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of possession proceedings stayed to determine Mrs Steinberg's Part 20 claim for declarations of life occupancy rights overriding the claimants' charge.
enrichment.outcome: Mrs Steinberg held to have a constructive trust life interest prior to the charging order but sale ordered with vacant possession if no buyer found within two months; life interest to be actuarially capitalised from proceeds.
enrichment.ratio: A gratuitous assurance of rent-free occupation for life, relied on by abstaining from blocking an undervalue intra-family transfer and signing mortgage consents, may impose a constructive trust binding later equitable chargees; such an interest can be an overriding interest, but the court may still order sale under TOLATA to realise secured creditors' claims.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Steinberg had a proprietary life interest in the flat
Whether a constructive trust or proprietary estoppel arose from 1981 arrangements
Priority of life interest over solicitors' equitable charge
Appropriate TOLATA relief balancing occupier and creditor interests

Williams & Glyn's Bank Ltd v Boland [1981] AC 487

notes: Illegal performance of employment contract appeal; Hall principles and EAT procedure point clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Employment claim barred for illegal tax performance without active participation
key_facts: Mrs Wheeler, a Thai cook with limited English, worked at a Sheffield restaurant receiving cash wages without tax or NI deductions.
The employment tribunal found illegal performance of the contract and dismissed unfair dismissal and payslip claims, though it would otherwise have upheld them.
The tribunal relied heavily on her husband's knowledge and acquiescence rather than clear findings against the employee.
The employer was in liquidation and did not appear; the tribunal raised illegality of its own motion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of appeal against employment tribunal decision on illegal contract performance.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; EAT decision quashed; matter remitted to employment tribunal for hearing on merits without rehearing on illegality.
enrichment.ratio: Under Hall v Woolston Hall, illegal performance of an otherwise lawful employment contract bars enforcement only if the employee knew the facts making performance illegal and actively participated; mere acquiescence or family awareness is insufficient; the EAT should not peremptorily reject grounds challenging factual findings without considering chairman's notes.
legal_issues: Whether the contract or its performance was illegal
Whether Mrs Wheeler actively participated in illegal tax evasion
Correct application of Hall v Woolston Hall principles
Whether the EAT fairly dealt with factual challenge grounds

notes: Fraud claim freezing and Norwich Pharmacal orders; arbitration stay and non-disclosure analysis detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Freezing and disclosure orders upheld pending arbitration in data-management fraud claim
key_facts: Corporate claimants sued former Spherion managers alleging fraud and mismanagement after a collapsed data-management venture funded through Glidepath/Jeimon.
Holland J granted without-notice freezing, disclosure and Norwich Pharmacal orders in March 2004; defendants later sought to set them aside after claimants conceded a stay to arbitration.
Multiple agreements contained ICC or English arbitration clauses; no arbitrator had yet been appointed.
Defendants alleged material non-disclosure regarding shareholders' agreement claims and spurious arguments against staying for arbitration.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to discharge interlocutory freezing, disclosure and Norwich Pharmacal orders and for return of documents after concession of stay to arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Applications to set aside orders dismissed; proceedings stayed to arbitration; s 18 arbitrator appointment application dismissed; defendants awarded costs of 5 May variation.
enrichment.ratio: The court retains inherent jurisdiction under the Supreme Court Act to grant interlocutory relief wider than s 44 Arbitration Act where arbitration is anticipated but not yet commenced; minor legal arguments advanced on without-notice applications do not necessarily amount to material non-disclosure; Norwich Pharmacal orders against third parties may be made before arbitral proceedings begin where tracing relief is needed.
legal_issues: Whether freezing and disclosure orders were made without jurisdiction once arbitration was conceded
Whether claimants materially misled the court on without-notice applications
Scope of inherent jurisdiction versus s 44 Arbitration Act 1996
Whether Norwich Pharmacal orders should be set aside

notes: Haulage operator licensing appeal; transport manager and Article 1 proportionality issues thoroughly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Revocation of haulage licences for absent transport manager control from Romania
key_facts: Anglorom, Paramount and Team Kitchens were related haulage companies controlled by Mr Ballestrieri using a Basildon operating centre.
Vehicle examiner evidence showed international operations were controlled from Romania with Mr Briggs nominally transport manager but excluded from day-to-day management.
Traffic Commissioner revoked all three licences and indefinitely disqualified Anglorom; Transport Tribunal allowed Team Kitchens' appeal only.
Non-EU drivers were used on British-registered vehicles within the EU but that point was not pursued.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Transport Tribunal upholding revocation of Paramount and Anglorom operator licences and Anglorom's disqualification.
enrichment.outcome: Paramount appeal dismissed; Anglorom appeal allowed only to set aside indefinite disqualification; no further extension of suspension of revocation orders.
enrichment.ratio: A company must employ a transport manager who continuously and effectively manages transport operations; delegating control to a director abroad means the statutory requirement is not met and revocation under section 27 follows as a matter of law rather than discretionary good repute balancing; a transport manager's good repute must be assessed separately from the company's; indefinite disqualification requires a clear balancing exercise which was not adequately reasoned.
legal_issues: Whether shared management between director and transport manager satisfied section 58
Whether loss of good repute and lack of professional competence were established
Article 1 proportionality of revocation and disqualification
Whether Mr Briggs' good repute was wrongly impugned

notes: Ancillary relief Barder application refused for delay; duty of candour and supervening value principles applied.

enrichment.short_title: Consent ancillary relief order not reopened after secret rapid sale at higher price
key_facts: Consent ancillary relief order of 20 July 1999 transferred Awbridge Danes to the husband on basis of £850,000 Savills valuation with lump sum to wife.
Within days the husband marketed the property and exchanged contracts in October 1999 for £1.7 million, completing before the order was perfected.
The wife knew by December 2000 that the property had sold for far more than the valuation but did not apply to reopen until February 2004.
She used the super-sale to accelerate lump sum payment and in satellite enforcement proceedings rather than seeking reassessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for extension of time and permission to appeal against refusal to set aside consent ancillary relief order for Barder/supervening event or breach of duty of candour.
enrichment.outcome: Extension of time refused; permission to appeal refused; consent order not reopened despite strong case that review was initially justified.
enrichment.ratio: A gross discrepancy between valuation at consent and actual sale price may justify reopening ancillary relief under Barder or for breach of the duty of full and frank disclosure, but a party who knows of the supervening event and uses it only to improve implementation of the order without promptly applying to reopen forfeits that remedy; delay of about three years after full knowledge is unreasonable.
legal_issues: Whether the husband breached the duty of candour at or after the consent hearing
Whether the rapid high-value sale was a Barder supervening event
Whether the wife applied reasonably promptly
Whether duty of candour continues after the consent order

notes: Combined judgment restating Newton hearing principles and deciding four sentencing appeals.

enrichment.short_title: Court of Appeal guidance on Newton hearings and disputed basis of plea

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: The court listed four appeals together to restate principles governing Newton hearings where guilty pleas rest on disputed facts.
Underwood was sentenced to five years after a Newton hearing on drug offer counts but the Crown had offered no evidence on a conspiracy count.
Khan's robbery sentence was reduced where the judge did not clearly resolve a disputed basis denying premeditation.
Connors' eight-year sentence for elderly-targeting burglary conspiracy was reduced to six years given his youth and driver role.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined appeals against sentence with lead judgment giving general procedural guidance on Newton hearings.
enrichment.outcome: Underwood sentence reduced to 3½ years; Khan to 4 years; Connors to 6 years; Arobieke application refused; general Newton guidance affirmed.
enrichment.ratio: Where disputed facts may materially affect sentence after a guilty plea, the judge may hold a Newton hearing; the Crown should not agree facts merely because it cannot gainsay them; sentencing must be on counts pleaded and accepted, not on wider uncharged conduct; acquiescence in a basis of plea is insufficient without knowledge and active participation where illegality is not in issue.
legal_issues: When a Newton hearing is required after guilty plea on disputed facts
Crown and judge roles in agreeing or rejecting a written basis of plea
Limits of Newton hearings including jury-only issues and mitigation
Effect of adverse Newton findings on guilty plea discount
linked_authorities: R v Newton (1983) 77 Cr App R 13

notes: Local authority land sale rectification claim; delegated powers authorisation analysis is central.

enrichment.short_title: Rectification refused over Barnet stadium sale 10-year development clawback error
key_facts: Barnet Council sold Underhill Football Ground freehold to Barnet FC Holdings for £10,000 with restrictive covenant and supplemental deed sharing future development value.

Negotiations in July 2001 intended unlimited football-use restriction and 60/40 split of development proceeds if the club left Barnet, but delegated powers report paragraph 11.4.4 introduced a 10-year cut-off.
Executed transfer and deed limited restrictive covenant and further consideration rights to 10 years.
Holdings argued the borough's intention must be taken from the authorised delegated powers report, not the negotiator Mr Stephens alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of rectification of transfer and supplemental deed in Chancery claim; section 123 voidness point not appealed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; rectification refused because the borough's intention was that authorised by the delegated powers report, not the July accord.
enrichment.ratio: For rectification of a local authority land disposal, the authority's intention is that of the body which gave formal authorisation, not the negotiating officer; where the sanctioned report can be read as authorising a 10-year cut-off, instruments reflecting that limit cannot be rectified to match an earlier unapproved accord; unilateral mistake requires sharp practice by the other party, not merely awareness of an internal drafting error.
legal_issues: Whether transfer and deed should be rectified to remove 10-year limits
Whose intention counts for a local authority rectification claim
Construction of the delegated powers report
Whether Holdings engaged in sharp practice knowing of the borough's mistake
linked_authorities: Joscelyne v Nissen [1970] 2 QB 93
Crane v Hegeman-Harris Co Inc [1945] KB 516

notes: Landmark software copyright judgment; look-and-feel and business-logic claims largely rejected; some GUI icon copying noted.

enrichment.short_title: Navitaire v easyJet: copyright in airline booking user interfaces
key_facts: Navitaire sued easyJet and developer BulletProof for infringing copyright in the OpenRes airline reservation system, principally its user interface and related works.
easyJet commissioned eRes to replicate OpenRes functionality without access to OpenRes source code; underlying code was entirely different.
Claims included non-textual copying of booking steps, VT100 and GUI screen layouts, TakeFlight web interface, database schemas, and reports.
easyJet had copied and modified TakeFlight Perl source for bug fixes; NIBS/easyJet.com did not copy TakeFlight source code.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of copyright infringement action concerning complex airline booking software.
enrichment.outcome: Claim largely failed: look-and-feel and business-logic non-textual copying rejected; trivial report layouts and functional database structures not substantial parts; limited GUI icon copying found but modest skill and labour; TakeFlight five-step booking sequence claim abandoned as non-textual copying.
enrichment.ratio: Copyright in a computer program does not protect the look and feel of its user interface, general business logic, or obvious booking sequences where no source code is copied; functional ideas underlying interfaces and commonplace screen elements are excluded; protection requires a substantial part of the skill and labour in the literary or artistic work itself, not similarity of function or trivial layouts.
legal_issues: Whether user interface appearance is a substantial part of copyright in program code
Non-textual or business-logic copying of software
Copyright in GUI screens as artistic works
Database schema and table structure as literary works
TakeFlight Perl module and web booking sequence
